paper_design_summary: In a controlled computer laboratory, 444 analyzed participants worked in 148 three-person teams on a written product-idea task with divergent search, convergent selection and final consolidation. Randomly formed teams were allocated through a randomized session sequence to five DeepSeek V3.2 access regimes: divergent stage only, convergent stage only, all stages, no AI, or divergent stage plus a warning. Four raters described as experts scored final proposals blind to condition; the primary team-level creativity composite combines originality, appropriateness and elaboration, while text quality, within-team semantic breadth, proposal count and diagnostic AI ratings are separate measures.

studies.label: Phase-contingent AI access in three-person teams (product-design task)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Randomly formed three-person teams were allocated sequentially to a fully randomized sequence of 150 planned condition-by-task sessions: five AI-access regimes crossed with three product-idea prompts. ai_tool.name_model: DeepSeek V3.2 via API, temperature 0.1 (PDF p. 22, S1.2).
ai_tool.how_used: Each member could independently query the integrated chat panel during enabled stages; team conversations were also streamed to the AI. A new API session was initialized for each team. The assistant had a specified role, but its prompt is referred to separate code documentation. The query panel was greyed out during disabled stages and absent throughout C4 (PDF p. 22, S1.2). Mean LLM calls per team ranged from 12.48 in C5 to 30.00 in C3 (PDF p. 27, Supplementary Table 1).

task.description: One written product/service concept task per team: combine a backpack with a pet accessory, a refrigerator with a calendar, or shoes with a map. Each member could draft proposals during the task; a team representative submitted a final document containing a product name, feature list and description, limited to 250 words. A document could contain multiple proposals. No drawing or visual-design output was required (PDF pp. 21-22, S1.1-S1.2).
task.duration: 40 minutes: 15 minutes divergent ideation, 15 minutes convergent selection, 10 minutes final consolidation/review and submission (PDF p. 21, S1.1).

outcomes.name: Human-rated team creativity composite (calibrated)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Four experts, blind to condition, scored every proposal; Creativity = 0.70 Originality + 0.15 Appropriateness + 0.15 Elaboration, with Originality = 0.9 Quality + 0.1 Quantity + Naming bonus. Averaged across proposals within a team, then across raters; rater-severity (MFRM-equivalent) calibration. ICC(2,k) = 0.421. Robustness: leave-one-rater-out, expert-only, mixed model, bootstrap (Supplementary Table 13, PDF p. 39); task-specific contrasts (Supplementary Table 14). Rubric and aggregation: PDF pp. 8 and 23-24, S1.6; reliability: PDF p. 37, Supplementary Table 11. Text quality is excluded from the composite (PDF p. 8, Human-rated creativity). Additional printed robustness results (PDF p. 39, Supplementary Table 13): expert-only Hedges g=0.926 [0.419, 1.543] for C1-C4 and 0.836 [0.340, 1.485] for C3-C4; mixed-model score-point b=0.507 [0.314, 0.700], p<0.001 for C1-C4 and b=0.453 [0.257, 0.650], p<0.001 for C3-C4. These are sensitivity analyses of the same outcome. The paper calls this outcome primary; the PDF does not establish preregistered primary-outcome status.

eligibility.reason: Final review confirms all three criteria for S1. Randomly formed teams were allocated through a fully randomized condition/task session sequence to generative-AI assistance regimes, including a no-AI control (PDF pp. 21-23, S1.1/S1.4). The analyzed sample contains 444 people in 148 teams; analyzed arm counts are 90, 90, 90, 87 and 87 people for C1-C5 (PDF p. 22, S1.1; p. 27, Supplementary Table 1). Four experts rated the submitted creative proposals blind to condition, and those output ratings form the primary team-level creativity score (PDF pp. 23-24, S1.6). C3 retained AI access throughout production and final submission; other AI arms had phase restrictions (PDF pp. 22-23, S1.2/S1.4). S1-O6 text quality is corrected to usefulness under codebook section 6; the correction does not change criterion 3. The unresolved reporting and coding details do not affect any eligibility criterion. Initial randomized people counts remain null, and team-level SDs and precision must not be treated as 444 independent outcome observations.

one_line_finding: Divergent-stage AI and full-process AI improved human-rated team creativity versus no AI (4.86 and 4.81 vs 4.35; Hedges g=0.81, p=0.00265 and g=0.77, p=0.00424), while convergent-only and warning-framed AI showed no clear improvement (g=0.25, p=0.328 and g=0.43, p=0.104; Supplementary Table 5, PDF p. 31).
open_questions: The paper describes four experts but does not identify the expert-only robustness subset or establish whether the rater labels YU and ZHOU identify authors. Do not infer author identity from surnames (PDF pp. 24, 37 and 39).
Supplementary Table 15 calls its parenthetical values dispersion without specifying SD or SE. Their type remains null/unconfirmed for semantic breadth, proposal count and character count (PDF p. 41).
The form vocabulary has no measure code for a computed character count. S1-O10 retains the observed length outcome and leaves measure null; a codebook decision is needed.
The original number of people randomized is not stated. Planned sessions and the analytic flow should not be substituted for that number (PDF pp. 21-22 and 28).

Outcome IDs follow screener A; screener B used a different ordering for originality, AI ratings, breadth and proposal count. Differences of order, equivalent wording, equivalent locators and moving the same statistic between a contrast and measure_detail are not counted as substantive differences. All nine outcomes listed by either screener are retained, with the additional descriptive character-count outcome. Originality-quantity and naming bonus are components of the originality rubric, with no separate treatment estimates printed; they are described in S1-O3. Stage-1 chat, AI-output provenance and AI-human rater divergence are process/evaluator diagnostics rather than additional creativity or across-person diversity outcomes. No outcome compares different teams for homogenization. Question coding is with_ai with mixed availability because the scored proposal is the product of one continuous ideation/drafting/selection task: personal drafts were produced during the task, and Stage 3 is final consolidation/submission (PDF pp. 21-22). C1/C5 lost query access after Stage 1 and C2 after Stage 2; only C3 retained it in Stage 3 (PDF p. 23), and no off-window queries were observed (PDF p. 63, Supplementary Figure 3). Submission after query withdrawal is not evidence that an independently scored new output was produced wholly without AI; no separate unassisted transfer task is reported. This coding does not claim AI was available at submission in C1/C2/C5. For a primary with_ai ai_vs_bau record, C3-C4 is the closest-to-free-chatbot contrast under codebook rule 8.3; the paper also emphasizes C1-C4. Planned contrast values follow Supplementary Table 5 (PDF p. 31), which matches the main text, rather than the discrepant caption to Supplementary Figure 5 (PDF p. 65: C1-C4 g=0.80, C2-C4 p=0.34, C5-C4 g=0.42, p=0.11). C5 adjusted and raw means are distinct in Table 12 (PDF p. 38: 4.643 and 4.653); this is a calibration difference, not two interchangeable estimates. No effect sizes, SEs or figure values were calculated. Simple descriptive means with unidentified dispersion have empty statistics_available lists because no precise code is offered.
